title: Heuristic KV warmup results & next-config sync
summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on KV/prefix cache warmup heuristics. Team reviewed last week's experiments (three variants), observed improvements in effective hit rate and cost but noticed increased tail latency for long-context sessions. Decided on follow-ups: run 48h synthetic traffic with session-affinity enabled, prune low-value prefixes, and finalize TTL/eviction knobs for production pilot. SE to share bench spreadsheet and config diff; AE to update pilot timeline and pricing assumptions.
topics: experiment results: baseline vs prefix-bucket vs template-normalization
prompt reuse normalization and dedup rules
warming strategies and synthetic run plan
eviction policy tradeoffs (LRU vs LFU vs segmenting by token-length)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-22 14:00 UTC, Duration 47m
Attendees: Ava Chen, Liam Patel (Redwood); Rachel Torres, Samir Kapoor, Eleni Ward (MosaicAI)

[00:00] Ava Chen: alright everyone thanks for hopping on, we want to go through the warmup heuristic results and the tuning recs. we'll try to keep it tight, uh, five sections: results, latency, prompt reuse, recommended config, next steps.

[00:28] Rachel Torres: great, I have about 40 minutes, thanks. excited to see where the hit rates landed.

[00:37] Liam Patel: yep, quick recap: we ran three variants over last 72 hours against your live-ish traffic mirror. baseline (no prefix grouping) gave approx 11.7% KV hit, prefix-bucket variant where we hash by first 12 tokens gave 33.9%, and template-normalization (we normalized user prompts and trim session-specific bits) gave 28.4% hit but lower tail latency. numbers are approximate, samples are in the bench sheet.

[01:12] Samir Kapoor: okay 33.9% is promising, what was the impact on token cost? did it change generate tokens per request?

[01:20] Liam Patel: good question. effective per-token compute dropped by ~18% on the prefix-bucket run because more requests hit the KV and avoided re-generation; however we did see an increase of 60-120ms P95 for sessions with long histories when cache lookup pipeline contended with batching on the GPU. so cost down, some tail latency tradeoff.

[02:01] Eleni Ward: can you clarify contention? is that a serving runtime issue or our traffic pattern?

[02:07] Liam Patel: a mix — the runtime serializes some KV-merge ops with the continuous-batching path; with more hits, we saw more small quick KV returns that interleave with large decode batches causing scheduling jitter. we flagged it for the infra team; meanwhile we recommend session-affinity to keep hot sessions on same worker which reduces cross-worker KV pulls.

[02:48] Rachel Torres: hmm, session-affinity sounds fine but we need to consider scale, will that blow up resource usage?

[02:55] Ava Chen: yeah, that's exactly why we propose a hybrid: session-affinity for top 10% of active sessions, otherwise default routing. that gives most of the benefit without full worker pinning.

[03:12] Samir Kapoor: what about eviction TTLs? we saw a lot of low-value prefixes polluting the cache in earlier runs.

[03:19] Liam Patel: we experimented with 3 TTL bands: short (5min) for single-turn queries, medium (1h) for multi-turn but low reuse, long (24h) for templates. pruning low entropy prefixes (like greetings) reduced noise. also suggested bloom-filter pre-check to avoid lookups for known-nonreusable queries.

[04:05] Rachel Torres: bloom filter, interesting — what's the false positive rate you tuned for?

[04:09] Liam Patel: tuned to ~1%, it's a cheap front-door, reduces lookups by about 7% without hurting hits.

[04:20] Eleni Ward: any change in model output quality from template normalization? sometimes normalizing can strip disambiguating context.

[04:29] Liam Patel: good point. we ran evals on 2500 held-out prompts; normalization caused negligible N-1 delta in quality metrics (BLEU-like scoring for structured tasks) but we flagged a small class of prompts where entity-level tokens were trimmed incorrectly. recommendation is to add entity-preserve rules to normalization.

[05:03] Rachel Torres: what's the plan to handle those exceptions? we can't have hallucinations from dropped context.

[05:10] Ava Chen: two steps — first, exclude entity-heavy prompts from normalization using simple heuristics (NER tag threshold). second, add an allowlist for enterprise doc IDs that should never be normalized. we can share the rule-set.

[05:35] Samir Kapoor: curious about the warmup strategy you mentioned earlier, like prefetching top-k prefixes during off-peak?

[05:41] Liam Patel: yes, we built a warmup job that prefetches top-k prefix vectors each hour. in the pilot this reduced cold-start misses by ~12% during morning spike. downside is some extra egress/compute; we recommend backfilling only top 0.5% of prefixes for cost control.

[06:12] Rachel Torres: and does warmup interact with eviction? like will we keep warming prefixes that should be evicted?

[06:19] Liam Patel: good catch — warmup uses a weight-decay table so warmed prefixes decay unless they cross an activity threshold. eviction policies respect warmup weights, so we avoid futile warming.

[06:40] Ava Chen: quick interruption — competition question that popped from our internal team: any concerns about customers switching to other managed providers because of these latency spikes?

[06:48] Eleni Ward: we did a short bake-off internally with Vertex and noticed consistent P95 stability there, but the KV hit rates were lower so cost was higher. we care about both latency SLO and cost.

[07:10] Liam Patel: fair, it's tradeoffs. for MosaicAI, we think hybrid routing + top-0.5% warmup + entity-aware normalization gets you to target cost without regressing latency SLA most of the time.

[07:28] Samir Kapoor: timeline? if we accept this config, what's next?

[07:33] Ava Chen: we recommended: SE runs a 48h synthetic at production QPS with session-affinity on top-10% and warmup. share bench sheet and config diffs. then a gated pilot (1 week) on 10% traffic. if metrics look good, roll to 50% then full.

[08:00] Rachel Torres: ok, let's schedule the synthetic, who owns that?

[08:04] Liam Patel: I will own the run, Samir will help provide the traffic mirror endpoints and allowlist.

[08:12] Samir Kapoor: yes happy to. we'll also need the config diff to check with compliance — any data retention changes?

[08:20] Ava Chen: no retention changes, just cache TTLs. nothing persisted to external systems beyond existing logs. we'll provide the config diff for review.

[08:31] Eleni Ward: can you also provide an emergency rollback plan if tail latency spikes after we increase traffic percent?

[08:37] Liam Patel: yes — we propose immediate fallback to baseline model variant (no KV) and automatic throttling; we've got playbook steps we'll share.

[08:48] Ava Chen: cool. quick note on pricing: with the expected hit-rate uplift, estimated monthly cpu/GPU cost reduction is ~23% for given workload. i'll update the pilot pricing doc and share.

[09:02] Rachel Torres: sounds good. any blockers from your side, Liam?

[09:07] Liam Patel: only that I need the traffic mirror credentials and a small allowlist of enterprise doc IDs to skip normalization.

[09:16] Samir Kapoor: sending creds today after call.

[09:20] Ava Chen: perfect. let's move to the recap and actions.

[09:25] [Auto-summary generator appears but imperfect]
[09:30] Speaker 1: summarized the key points: 1) prefix-bucket increased hit rate to ~34%, 2) template-normalization gave 28% with lower tail, 3) recommended hybrid routing + top-0.5% warmup + entity-preserve rules.

[09:52] Rachel Torres: thanks, that aligns with our notes. can you also share the bench csv and the config diff as a PR?

[10:01] Liam Patel: yes uploading to your shared drive; will ping here.

[10:10] Ava Chen: ok final anything else?

[10:14] Eleni Ward: just one more — can we add a quick check in 2 days to confirm run started?

[10:19] Ava Chen: sure, 48 hour run starts Wednesday, we'll check in Friday.

[10:25] Meeting end: thanks all.

Notes on quality: there are a few mis-transcribed bits (runtime vs routing) in the auto-gen, please check the bench sheet for exact numbers.
